sections.html:
• Name: Arrow crab
  • Other names: Yellowline arrow crab, Majoid crab, Caribbean spider crab, Caribbean ghost crab
  • Scientific name: Stenorhynchus seticornis
  • Minimum tank size: 20 gallons (~80 litres)
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Carapace size: up to 3–4 cm
  • Leg span: 15 cm
  • Water: SG 1.021–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 7–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: mostly carnivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: semi-aggressive
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour: whitish or light tan with fine dark/brown lines

The Arrow crab is an interesting addition to a home aquarium. It is a great scavenger, will control bristleworms in the tank, and is very hardy and easy to care for.

However, people love getting Arrow crabs for their saltwater aquariums because of how cool these alien creatures can be, and impulse purchases of invertebrates are common without realising the potential consequences. Their semi-aggressive nature limits the options in a community tank, as they may attack other crabs, fish, snails and shrimp.

The Arrow crab is a common and widely distributed inhabitant of the Caribbean Sea and the western Atlantic Ocean, from the intertidal zone to 200 m in depth. It ranges along the west Atlantic coasts, from North Carolina to Argentina.

The Arrow crab lives on a variety of bottoms: rocks, corals, seaweed beds, pebbles, sand, or sand mixed with broken shell, wharf pilings and rock jetties. It is one of the most diverse crab species when it comes to the environment.

Being somewhat large for a saltwater crab, the Arrow crab requires a substantial amount of space. Nano reef tanks are out of the question. An Arrow crab needs at least a 20-gallon (80-litre) tank per individual.

If you plan to keep two, a 200-litre tank might do, provided they are not both male, as males will fight to the death.

Because of their hardiness, Arrow crabs are very easy to care for. The only problem is the tank size.

Your tank should have plenty of rocks and caves for the crab to hide in. This is crucial for its well-being.

Consistent water parameters are the cornerstone of any successful aquarium. Make sure they are all kept within a suitable range at all times and do not jump around.

Before putting an Arrow crab in your tank, acclimate it, as with all invertebrates.

Be careful with chemicals like copper. Crabs, shrimp and crayfish do not tolerate copper-based medications or fluctuating water parameters.

Arrow crabs do not need any additional supplements to survive in captivity, but tank water must be kept warm, between 22 and 28°C, with 24–27°C being optimal.

Calcium concentration, pH and alkalinity must also be maintained at acceptable levels. A calcium concentration of 400–450 ppm is optimal, but it can be a bit lower or higher. The pH should be kept around 8.1–8.4 and alkalinity in the range of 7–12 dKH, although these often go a little higher or lower.

Salinity: SG 1.021–1.025. Nitrate: less than 20 ppm.
Basic tank equipment: filter, air pump, heater, substrate, live rock, sea salt, test kits and a hydrometer or salinity refractometer.

One of the best (and unfortunately the worst) things about Arrow crabs is that they are opportunistic omnivores. They will eat anything they can catch, including other motile invertebrates, mollusks, small fish and other living organisms smaller than themselves.

Although these crabs are not fussy eaters, it would be wrong to think they do not require a specific diet. Keep them fed all the time and do not let them get hungry.

It is not guaranteed, but when well fed, Arrow crabs can in general become more tolerant of tank mates. That is why some aquarists supplement their diet about 3–4 times a week (for example mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, squid, phytoplankton, zooplankton, enriched flakes, seaweed, etc.).

Arrow crabs are generally safe with hardy native corals and anemones. They will not bulldoze through corals like big crabs often do. However, they are omnivores and may start picking at corals if not given enough food. Keep an eye on the crab for the first week or so, and do not let it get hungry.

Both in the wild and in the aquarium, Arrow crabs are nocturnal. By day they prefer well-protected locations in crevices, holes or between the tentacles or arms of crinoids, actinians and sea anemones. In the evening they start climbing up the coral head, looking for exposed locations. At night they can be found in exposed locations, on soft corals or gorgonians.

They actively feed only at night and dawn, not during the day. At dawn they descend from the soft corals and return to their daytime location. This diurnal rhythm seems to be a sort of negative phototaxis. Once Arrow crabs adapt to a new environment and feeding regime, they can slightly change their night/day behaviour and come out a lot more during the day.

Although Arrow crabs are slow-moving, they have a semi-aggressive temperament. Arrow crabs, especially males, are territorial and very aggressive to each other, and will fight for territory and dominance. In a small tank it is better to keep only one crab.

Their aggression is latent until they grow to adult size. At this point they may become aggressive and can attack small prey in the tank, such as invertebrates and even small fish.

Arrow crabs are not shy and can be easily approached, obviously relying on camouflage as a defence.

In nature, adult crabs seem to migrate into deeper water. There are no obvious predators of Stenorhynchus seticornis. Arrow crabs clean the reef of organic matter and serve as scavengers of the coral heads.

Tank mates. Arrow crabs are not completely safe and peaceful with other tank mates. They can become pretty aggressive the older and bigger they get, so it is risky to house them with small and peaceful fish, shrimp and snails, which they will likely eventually prey on.

Some aquarists keep them with relatively large shrimp such as peppermint shrimp, red fire shrimp, skunk cleaner shrimp, camel shrimp, etc. This is not a good idea: Arrow crabs have very sharp claws, which in the best-case scenario can easily damage the antennae or legs of the shrimp.

Snails (cerith snails, bumble bee snails, conch snails, nassarius snails, etc.) and small hermit crabs (Halloween hermit crabs, blue leg hermit crabs, etc.) can also be on their menu. They move very slowly, making them ideal prey.

Coral banded shrimp are also not recommended: they are also territorial and aggressive. Their size lets them fight back, but they will eventually lose the battle if things get serious.

Full-grown emerald crabs should not worry about Arrow crabs; the size of the crab plays a huge role here.

Do not keep Arrow crabs with aggressive fish such as groupers, lionfish, eels and triggerfish, as they will prey on them. The extreme length of the legs makes the crabs difficult to eat at first, but once the crab loses most of its legs, it becomes easy prey.

In essence, you would do no harm by keeping an Arrow crab alone.

It is rather easy to tell male and female Arrow crabs apart.

  • In males the abdomen has a triangular shape; in females it is wider and rounder.
  • Males are also a little bigger and have larger claws than females.

Stenorhynchus seticornis is heavily harvested for ornamental purposes, so it is extremely important to develop large-scale rearing methods. The following is a compilation of facts from several studies.

Under good conditions, Arrow crabs can breed all year round. After mating, females produce large eggs (0.48–0.57 mm) in small clutches. Berried females carry the eggs on their abdomen until they hatch a few weeks later. In general, a female carries about 300–900 eggs. There is a significant correlation between the number of eggs per brood and the size of ovigerous females; the size of the breeding female has been pointed out as a key variable determining the number of eggs extruded per batch. According to one study, the weight of the egg mass is usually limited to about 10% of the female's weight.

Eggs increase in volume during development as a result of water uptake. This increase limits the available egg-carrying space, resulting in smaller broods.

Optimal conditions for breeding

Larval development occurs within a well-defined range of environmental conditions characteristic of the species. Of the environmental factors that affect crustacean development, temperature and salinity significantly affect survival and the duration of larval life.

  • Larvae need a separate rearing tank. Light attracts the larvae, so you can lure them to a spot in the tank corner with a flashlight or adjustable desk spot lamp, then catch them with a turkey baster or a big syringe.
  • If you already have a separate tank, remove the females from the rearing tank after the eggs hatch.
  • According to the study, the highest mean survival from hatching to the first crab stage (4.5%) occurred at 25°C, salinity 30‰, photoperiod of 10 h light/14 h dark and pH 8.1–8.4. Survival declines more steeply at 28°C at all salinities. At 22°C, larvae needed longer (27–35 days) to complete development to the first crab.
  • When moving larvae from the main tank to the rearing tank, as a precaution against thermal shock, acclimate them slowly by gradually lowering or raising the temperature (about 1 degree per hour).
  • Feeding is extremely important. Larvae cannot recover from nutritional stress caused by previous starvation even if they are fed afterwards (the 'point of no return'). In addition, a lack of food of proper size and nutritional value when larvae first begin feeding causes extensive mortality.
  • Feed the larvae daily (ideally twice) on newly hatched Artemia nauplii (approximately 5 nauplii per ml).
  • To avoid salinity changes in the rearing setup, screen and rinse the nauplii with filtered seawater at the necessary salinity.
  • Water parameters should be stable. Remove any detritus from the tank.

Larval development

Early postembryonic development of Stenorhynchus seticornis consists of two zoeal stages before the megalopa stage. The babies are called zoeae; once born they swim towards the surface and feed on small plankton.

First zoea stage: mean survival is less than 61% under all experimental conditions. Depending on the temperature, the stage lasts 3–5 days (28°C–22°C).

Second zoea stage: mean survival varied from 26% at 28°C, 35‰ to 6% at 25°C, 30‰. Depending on the temperature, the stage lasts 3–6 days (28°C–22°C).

Megalopa stage: this stage shows the highest mortality. Survival is lower than 12% under optimal conditions (25°C, 30‰). Depending on the temperature, the stage lasts 18–24 days (22°C–28°C).

Cumulative survival from hatching to the first crab stage is very low (only 3–4%). In nature, however, larval survival is generally even lower, often less than 1%. The reasons for the high mortality of megalopae remain unsolved.

Description

At first glance, Arrow crabs look more like underwater spiders than crabs. The species is appreciated by aquarists for its extremely long, spider-like legs and small triangular body the size of a dime. The spindly legs can reach 10–15 cm long.

Arrow crabs have a spear-like rostrum (spike on the head) that sticks out between two beady eyes. The carapace is whitish or light tan with fine dark/brown lines running from the median line to the margin. Full-grown, an adult's carapace is only around 3 cm. The rostrum is long and narrow (up to 3 cm), drawn out into a tapered point.

The long, slender legs are often spotted or banded with orange or red. Arrow crabs have blue to violet claws that look more like gloves. In captivity they can live up to 5 years.

Cleaning behaviour

A paper reports the yellowline arrow crab acting as a cleaner of longjaw squirrelfish (Holocentrus adscencionis) and moray eels (Gymnothorax funebris, G. moringa, G. vicinus) at two reefs in the Baía de Todos os Santos, Bahia State, eastern Brazil. Biologists believe other reef fish are potential 'clients' of the Arrow crab and that this activity occurs throughout its distribution.

Association with urchins

Researchers studied the host selection of Arrow crabs with the long-spined urchin Diadema antillarum in the shallow coastal waters of Tobago. Because the crabs paid no attention to shorter-spined urchins, they concluded that the longer, mildly toxic spines of D. antillarum afforded more protection from potential predators than the spines of other available urchin hosts. Whether Arrow crabs identify Diadema antillarum by visual, tactile or olfactory cues (or a combination) remains uncertain.

This association is not a symbiosis: Arrow crabs do not require urchins all the time, and the urchin apparently derives no benefit from the crab.

Moulting

Like all crustaceans, Arrow crabs need to moult (shed their shells) to grow. Moulting is a key stage in the life cycle of any crab, shrimp, crayfish, lobster, etc., and indicates healthy growth.

Although the moult itself usually lasts only a few minutes, it takes weeks for a crab to prepare. A few days before moulting, Arrow crabs move even slower than usual and do not eat as much. During this time they start pumping up water to break the old shell and withdraw from it.

Arrow crabs are extremely vulnerable in this soft-shell phase and need a safe place to hide while their shells harden, which is another reason to keep enough rocks and hiding spots in the tank.

Tip: do not throw away old shells. They contain lots of minerals and the crabs will gladly eat them after some time.

Like all invertebrates, Arrow crabs need calcium to mineralise (harden) the shell. Calcium is vital for good shell growth.

Bristleworms, feather dusters and vermetids

Many marine aquarists complain about bristleworms in the sandbed or in algae clumps growing on rocks. These worms are small and almost impossible to notice until you see bunches of them swarming. In this case the Arrow crab can be a solution, as it is very effective against bristleworms. However, before introducing one you need to understand the temper and feeding preferences of the species.

Most of these worms are beneficial scavengers and efficient detritus consumers that do no harm to a marine system. All bristleworms were jinxed by one notorious species (Hermodice carunculata, the bearded fireworm), so most hobbyists consider them all pests and try to remove them immediately, which is not justified. Weigh all the pros and cons before adding an Arrow crab, otherwise the cure can become worse than the disease.

Lots of bristleworms is a sign of excessive detritus and dissolved nutrients in the tank. Revise feeding and stocking, do maintenance, clean the substrate and do a water change.

Regarding vermetid snails ('tubeworms'), there is a rumour that Arrow crabs can control their population. This is an exaggeration: if possible, Arrow crabs prefer to eat something tastier and easier to catch. Arrow crabs will also eat all kinds of worms, including feather dusters, so be careful.
